en: Paying attention; noticing, watching, listening, or attending closely.
Courteous; mindful.

attentive.ety: From Middle English attentif, attentijf, from Old French attentif.

ex.en: They were most attentive to his speech.
ex.ja: みんなは彼の話を注意深く聞いた。

ex.en: Mary is very attentive, isn't she?
ex.ja: メアリーはとても気が利くよね。

ex.en: The listeners stood in an attentive attitude.
ex.ja: 聴衆は謹聴の姿勢で立っていた。

note.ja: at（〜へ）+ tent（伸ばす）+ ive。心を〜へ向けている →「注意深い・気配りのある」。

en: A field, stadium or park where ball, especially baseball, is played.
The general vicinity; somewhere close; a broad approximation.
Approximate; close; on the right order of magnitude.
To make a rough estimate of.

ballpark.ety: From ball + park. Sense 2 related to ballpark figure.

ex.en: He showed me the way to the ballpark.
ex.ja: 彼は私に球場への道を教えてくれた。

ex.en: You can go to the ballpark on this bus.
ex.ja: このバスに乗れば球場へ行けます。

ex.en: Could you tell me how to get to the ballpark?
ex.ja: 野球場にどうやって行ったらよいか教えていただけませんか。

note.ja: ball（球）+ park（場所）。「野球場」→ 球場の範囲内 →「概算（ballpark figure）」。

en: Relating to people, countries, or customs perceived as uncivilized or inferior.
A non-Greek or a non-Roman citizen.

ex.ja: 文明人も一皮むけば野蛮人。

en: A rigid structure projecting from the front of a bird's face, used for pecking, grooming, foraging, carrying items, eating food, etc.
A similar pointed structure forming the nose and mouth of various animals, such as turtles, platypuses, whales, etc.
To strike with the beak.
To seize with the beak.

beak.ety: From Middle English bec, borrowed from Anglo-Norman bec, Old French bec, from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos (“beak, snout”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *bak-, *baḱ- (“pointed stick, peg”). Cognate with Breton beg (“beak”). Compare Saterland Frisian Bäk (“mouth; muzzle; beak”); Dutch bek (“beak; bill; neb”).

ex.en: Woodpeckers peck tree trunks with their long pointed beaks and eat insects found there.
ex.ja: きつつきは、長く尖ったくちばしで、木の幹をつついて、中にいる虫を食べます。

note.ja: 古フランス語 bec（くちばし）から。ケルト語に由来する。

en: A colour, variously defined from a pale brown, to a yellow greyish off-white.
Debeige; a kind of woollen or mixed dress goods.
Having a slightly yellowish gray colour, as that of unbleached wool.
Comfortably dull and unadventurous, in a way that suggests middle-class suburbia.

beige.ety: Unadapted borrowing from French (dialectal) beige, from Old French bege (“color of undyed wool or cotton”), from an Alpine language (compare Franco-Provençal bézho, Romansch besch (“dull grey”)), from Vulgar Latin *bysseus (“cottony grey”) (compare French bis, Catalan bis, Italian bigio), from Late Latin byssus (“cotton”), from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “cotton homespun”), from Semitic (compare Hebrew/Aramaic בוץ (būṣ)). Doublet of bice.

ex.en: She stained the wall beige.
ex.ja: 彼女は壁をベージュ色にした。

note.ja: フランス語 beige（未染色の羊毛の色）から。

en: An act of irreverence or contempt toward a god or toward something considered sacred; an impious act, utterance, view, etc.
An act of irreverence towards anything considered inviolable; the act of disregarding a convention.

blasphemy.ety: From Middle English blasfemie, from Old French blasfemie, from Ecclesiastical Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “profanity”), from βλασφημέω (blasphēméō, “to slander”). Displaced native Old English tāl.

ex.en: "Novels? I hate novels." Oh muse, forgive her blasphemy.
ex.ja: 「小説？　あたし小説は嫌ひですの」 　おゝ、ミュウズよ、彼女の冒涜を赦せ。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 blasphēmia（冒涜）から。blaptein（害する）+ phēmē（言葉）。「神をののしる言葉」。blame と同じ語源。

ex.ja: ブルーベリーをとった後、タルトを作る。

A male pig.

boar.ety: From Middle English bor, boor, from Old English bār, from Proto-West Germanic *bair.

A field officer of the highest grade, below general officers, NATO grade OF-7.

To praise or acclaim.

To converse together with sympathy and confidence; to interchange sentiments or feelings; to take counsel.
To communicate (with) spiritually; to be together (with); to contemplate or absorb.

en: Pertaining to a conclusion.
Providing an end to something; decisive.

conclusive.ety: From French conclusif, from Late Latin conclusivus, from Latin conclūsīvē (“conclusively”), from past participle of concludere.

note.ja: con（完全に）+ clus（閉じる）+ ive。完全に閉じる →「決定的な・確実な」。

A school or clinic for orphans.
A music school.

Scattered or spread out.

en: A sudden or unexpected failure.
A ludicrous or humiliating situation. Some effort that went quite wrong.

Borrowed from Italian fiasco (“bottle, flask”), from Late Latin flasca, flascō (“bottle, container”), from Frankish *flaskā (“bottle, flask”) from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle”); see flask.
“Failure” sense comes through French faire fiasco from Italian theatrical slang far fiasco (literally “to make a bottle”), of uncertain origin; perhaps from an expression fare il fiasco, meaning to play a game with the forfeit that the loser will buy the next bottle or round of drinks.
Doublet of flacon, flagon, and flask.

ex.en: We'll never live this fiasco down.
ex.ja: この失敗、きっと一生、言われつづけるなあ。

note.ja: イタリア語 fiasco（瓶）から。far fiasco（瓶を作る）がガラス職人の失敗を指したことからとされる。「大失敗」。flask と同じ。

en: A state of terror excited by the sudden appearance of danger; sudden and violent fear, usually of short duration; a sudden alarm.
Someone strange, ugly or shocking, producing a feeling of alarm or aversion.

fright.ety:
From Middle English fright, furht, from Old English fryhtu, fyrhto (“fright, fear, dread, trembling, horrible sight”), from Proto-Germanic *furhtį̄ (“fear”), from Proto-Indo-European *pr̥k- (“to fear”).
Cognate with Scots fricht (“fright”), Old Frisian fruchte (“fright”), Low German frucht (“fright”), Middle Dutch vrucht, German Furcht (“fear, fright”), Danish frygt (“fear”), Swedish fruktan (“fear, fright, dread”), Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌷𐍄𐌴𐌹 (faurhtei, “fear, horror, fright”). Compare possibly Albanian frikë (“fear, fright, dread, danger”).

ex.en: The loud noise gave me a terrible fright.
ex.ja: 大きな物音で私は肝をつぶした。

ex.en: Such was her fright that she closed her eyes.
ex.ja: あまりの怖さに彼女は目を閉じた。

ex.en: Fright gave the old lady heart failure.
ex.ja: 突然の恐怖に老婆は心臓麻痺を起こした。

note.ja: 古英語 fyrhto（恐怖）から。「恐怖」。frighten と同じ。

en: Favourable to the growth of fruit or useful vegetation; not barren.
Being productive in any sense; yielding benefits.

fruitful.ety: From Middle English fruitefull, equivalent to fruit + -ful. Compare Dutch vruchtvol, German fruchtvoll, Swedish fruktfull.

ex.en: Their year-long stay in Germany was very fruitful.
ex.ja: ドイツに滞在した１年間は非常に実りの多いものだった。

ex.en: Their stay in Germany for a year was very fruitful.
ex.ja: ドイツに滞在した１年間は非常に実りの多いものだった。

ex.en: I hope that your business trip to France was fruitful.
ex.ja: フランス出張が実り多きものであるといいね。

note.ja: fruit（成果）+ -ful。「実りの多い」。

en: Impudence or brazenness; temerity; chutzpah.
Great misery or physical suffering, likened to the bitterest-tasting of substances.
To chafe, to rub or subject to friction; to create a sore on the skin.
To bother or trouble.

gall.ety:
From Middle English galle, from Old English ġealla, galla, from Proto-West Germanic *gallā, from Proto-Germanic *gallǭ.
The figurative senses (e.g., impudence, brazenness, chutzpah) are related to the literal sense (i.e., bile) via the lasting linguocultural effects of humorism, which governed Western medicine for many centuries before the advent of scientific medicine.
Related to Dutch gal, German Galle, Swedish galle, galla, Ancient Greek χολή (kholḗ). Also remotely related with yellow and gold.

ex.en: For gall bladder surgery, go down this hall and take a right.
ex.ja: 胆のうの手術でしたら、この廊下をずっと行って右に曲がってください。

ex.en: His sarcasm galls me.
ex.ja: 彼の当てこすりはかんにさわる。

note.ja: 「胆汁」は古英語 gealla、yellow と同じ祖先。苦い胆汁 →「厚かましさ」。

en: Of or relating to the stomach.

gastric.ety: From New Latin gastricus, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ, γαστρός (gastḗr, gastrós, “stomach”). By surface analysis, gastr- + -ic; Doublet of gastrique.

ex.en: Too much alcohol may result in gastric disease.
ex.ja: 飲みすぎると胃の病気になるかもしれません。

ex.en: He died of gastric cancer.
ex.ja: 彼は胃ガンで死んだ。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 gastēr（胃）から。gastronomy（美食）と同じ。

en: To shine light on something.
To decorate something with lights.
Enlightened spiritually, divinely taught or inspired; in technical use, converted, baptized.
Someone thought to have an unusual degree of enlightenment.

illuminate.ety: From Middle English illuminaten, borrowed from Latin illūminātus, perfect passive participle of illūminō (“lighten, light up, show off”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from in + lūminō (“light up”), from lūmen (“light”). Cognate with Old English lȳman (“to glow, shine”). More at leam.

ex.ja: お日さまがその光で万事を照らします。

en: Not able to be accessed; out of reach; inconvenient.
Not able to be reached; unattainable.

inaccessible.ety: From Middle French inaccessible, from Late Latin inaccessibilis, equivalent to in- + accessible. Piecewise doublet of unaccessible.

ex.en: He is inaccessible to his employees.
ex.ja: 彼は従業員と打ち解けない。

A large fire; a conflagration.

inferno.ety:

The meaning "big fire" came as a figurative use from the traditional idea of hellfire.

note.ja: イタリア語 inferno（地獄）から。ラテン語 infernus（下の）。ダンテの『神曲』地獄篇。「地獄・大火」。inferior と同じ。

en: An energetic trot, slower than a run, often used as a form of exercise.
A sudden push or nudge.
To push slightly; to move or shake with a push or jerk, as to gain the attention of; to jolt.
To shake, stir or rouse.

jog.ety:
Of uncertain origin. Originally with the meaning of "to shake up and down." Possibly from Middle English joggen, a variant of jaggen (“to pierce, prod, stir up, arouse”); see jag (“sharp projection”).
Or, perhaps an early alteration of English shog (“to jolt, shake; depart, go”), from Middle English shoggen, schoggen (“to shake up and down, jog”), from Middle Dutch schocken (“to jolt, bounce”) or Middle Low German schoggen, schocken (“to shog”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *skukkōn (“to move, shake, tremble”), possibly related to *skakan (“to shake, stir”). More at shock.

ex.en: My uncle said that he jogs every morning.
ex.ja: おじは毎朝ジョギングしていると言った。

ex.en: I make it a rule to jog every morning.
ex.ja: 私は毎朝走ることにしている。

ex.en: We jog before breakfast every morning.
ex.ja: 私たちは毎朝食前にジョギングをする。

note.ja: shog（揺する）の変化形とされる。「軽く押す」→「ジョギングする・記憶を呼び起こす」。

en: A serving vessel or container, typically circular in cross-section and typically higher than it is wide, with a relatively small mouth or…

To stew in an earthenware jug etc.
To utter a sound like "jug", as certain birds do, especially the nightingale.

jug.ety: From Middle English jugge, of uncertain origin. Possibly a variant of Middle English jubbe, jobbe, iubbe, geobbe, itself of unknown origin; or perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English ċēac (“pitcher; jug”). Compare also jug (“a low woman, maidservant”), from Jug, familiar form of Joanna. Prison sense attested from at least 1825 in Britain.

ex.en: They filled the jug to the brim.
ex.ja: 彼らは水瓶を縁まで一杯にした。

note.ja: 語源ははっきりしない。女性の名 Joan の愛称 Jug からとする説がある。「水差し」。

chariot.ety: From Middle English chariot, from Old French chariot, from char (“cart”), from Latin carrus (“wagon”), itself borrowed from Gaulish *karros, from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥sós. Displaced native Old English hrædwæġn (literally “fast wagon”).

note.ja: 古フランス語 char（車）+ 拡大。ラテン語 carrus（荷車）。car と同じ語源。

en: Any of several acute infectious diseases of humans and domestic animals, caused by certain strains of the Vibrio cholerae bacterium throu…

cholera.ety: From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “cholera”). Doublet of choler.

ex.en: Two hundred people died of cholera last year.
ex.ja: ２００人の人が昨年コレラで死んだ。

ex.en: There have been many cases of cholera this year.
ex.ja: 今年はコレラ患者が多発した。

ex.en: There has been another case of cholera in the neighborhood.
ex.ja: 近所でまたもう１人のコレラ患者が出た。

note.ja: ギリシャ語 kholera（胆汁の病）から。kholē（胆汁）。cholesterol と同じ。

en: To bend and hammer the point of (a nail) so it cannot be removed.
To clasp; to interlock.
Any of several fastenings.
The act of bending and hammering the point of a nail so it cannot be removed.

ex.en: Now is the time to clinch the deal.
ex.ja: 今こそ一気に取引をまとめるときだ。

ex.en: He clinched the election when he came out against a tax increase.
ex.ja: 彼は増税反対の立場をとったことで、選挙戦に決着をつけました。

note.ja: clench（握りしめる）の変化形。「（釘を）打ち曲げる」→「（勝利を）確実にする」。

en: To make a direct impact, especially if violent.
To come into conflict, or be incompatible.

collide.ety: From Latin collīdō (“to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together”), from con- (“together”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence col- (“assimilated form of com-”)).

ex.en: Her car collided with a bus from behind.
ex.ja: 彼女の車はバスに追突した。

ex.en: The two cars collided with a crash.
ex.ja: ２台の車は激しい音を立てて衝突した。

ex.en: Our bus collided with a truck.
ex.ja: 私たちのバスがトラックと衝突した。

note.ja: ラテン語 collidere ＝ col（共に）+ laedere（打つ）。「ぶつかり合う」→「衝突する」。collision と同じ。

en: The act of commemorating; an observance or celebration to honor the memory of some person or event.
That which serves the purpose of commemorating; a memorial.

commemoration.ety: First attested in 1384, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English commemoracioun, from Old French commemoration (French commémoration), from Latin commemorātiō. By surface analysis, commemorate + -ion

note.ja: com（共に）+ memor（覚えている）+ ation。皆で思い起こすこと →「記念・記念式典」。

en: The quality, colour, or appearance of the skin on the face.
The outward appearance of something.
To give a colour to.

complexion.ety: From Middle English complexion (“temperament”), from Old French complexion (French complexion), from Medieval Latin complexiō (“complexion, constitution”), from complector, past participle complexus (“to entwine, encompass”).

ex.en: It puts a different complexion on the situation.
ex.ja: それにより状況が変る。

ex.en: She has a fair complexion.
ex.ja: 彼女は色白だ。

ex.en: You have a nice complexion.
ex.ja: 顔色いいね。

note.ja: com（共に）+ plex（編む）+ ion。（体液の）組み合わさり具合 →「顔色・肌の色・様相」。

en: Uncontrolled or reactive and irresistible.
Having power to compel; exercising or applying compulsion.
One who exhibits compulsive behaviours.

compulsive.ety: Borrowed from French compulsif, formed from Latin compulsus, past participle of compellere (“to compel”), from com- (“together”) + pellere (“to drive”).

ex.en: Once a habit has been acquired, it almost has compulsive power over us.
ex.ja: 一度習慣が身につけば、それはわれわれに対してほとんど強制的な力を持つ。

note.ja: compulsion（強制）+ -ive。com + pellere（駆り立てる）。compel と同じ pel。

en: Of or pertaining to a consul, or the office thereof.
A Roman ex-consul.

consular.ety: From Middle English consular, from Latin cōnsulāris. By surface analysis, consul + -ar.

note.ja: consul（領事）+ -ar。ラテン語 consul（古代ローマの執政官）。

en: Of or pertaining to correction; serving to correct.
Something that corrects or counteracts something.

corrective.ety: Borrowed from French correctif, equivalent to correct + -ive.

note.ja: correct（正す）+ -ive。「矯正の」。

en: To fall apart; to disintegrate.
To break into crumbs.
A dessert of British origin containing stewed fruit topped with a crumbly mixture of fat, flour, and sugar.

crumble.ety: From earlier crymble, crimble, from Middle English *crymblen, kremelen, from Old English *crymlan (“to crumble”), from *crymel (“a small crumb; crumble”), diminutive of Old English cruma (“crumb”), equivalent to crumb + -le (diminutive suffix). Compare Dutch kruimelen (“to crumble”), German Low German krömmeln (“to crumble”), German Krümel, diminutive of German Krume, German krümeln, krümmeln (“to crumble”). Alteration of vowel due to analogy with crumb.

ex.en: The building crumbled to pieces three years ago.
ex.ja: その建物は三年前に崩壊した。

ex.en: That's the way the cookie crumbles.
ex.ja: 人生とはそんなものさ。

ex.en: Recently, I've been suffering from lack of sleep, so my skin is crumbling.
ex.ja: 最近、睡眠不足だったから、お肌がボロボロ。

note.ja: crumb（パンくず）+ -le。「ぼろぼろに崩れる」。

en: Suspended from above.
In a state of suspense.
The act of hanging something so that it can move freely; suspension.
The act of following or trailing around.

ex.en: He sat on a chair with his legs dangling.
ex.ja: 彼は両足をぶらぶらさせながらいすに座っていた。

ex.en: His company is dangling by a thread. That's the rumor I hear.
ex.ja: 彼の会社、最近結構危ない橋を渡っているって、もっぱらの噂だよ。

note.ja: dangle（ぶら下がる）+ -ing。北欧語に由来する。

鋌而走險的人 /铤而走险的人

Recklessly bold; adventurous.
To behave in a reckless, adventurous, or physically risky manner.

daredevil.ety: From dare + devil; an exocentric compound, "one who dares the devil".

ex.en: He is a daredevil.
ex.ja: あいつは無鉄砲な男だ。

note.ja: dare（あえてする）+ devil（悪魔）。「悪魔をも恐れない」→「向こう見ずな人」。

Someone who washes dishes, especially one hired to wash dishes in a restaurant.

To draw or scribble aimlessly.
To engage in something non-seriously; fiddle.

The meaning "fool, simpleton" is intended in the song title "Yankee Doodle", originally sung by British colonial troops prior to the American Revolutionary War. This is also the origin of the early eighteenth century verb to doodle, me

ex.en: Do you ever doodle on a piece of paper when you're bored?
ex.ja: 退屈しているときに、紙に落書きをしたことがありませんか？

ex.en: Cock-a-doodle-doo!
ex.ja: コケコッコー！

note.ja: ドイツ語 Dudeldopp（まぬけ）から。「まぬけ」→「ぼんやり描く落書き」。

ex.en: We must eradicate the drug traffic, root and branch.
ex.ja: 麻薬の密売は根こそぎ絶やさなければならない。

ex.en: The savage in man is never quite eradicated.
ex.ja: 人間の野蛮性は決して根絶できない。

ex.ja: 我々は人種差別を完全に無くす努力を必ず続けて行く。

note.ja: ラテン語 eradicare（根こそぎにする）から。e（外へ）+ radix（根）。「根絶する」。radical と同じ。

A domesticated (non-human) animal that has returned to the wild; an animal, particularly a domesticated animal, living independently of h…
A contemptible young person, a lout, a person who behaves wildly.

feral.ety: From Latin fera (“wild beast”, noun) + -al or Latin ferus (“wild; savage; cruel”, adjective) + -al. Alternatively, borrowed from Middle French féral or Late Latin ferālis.

To store (an aircraft) in a hangar.

hangar.ety: Borrowed from French hangar (“shed, hangar”), from Middle French hanghart (“enclosure near a house”), from Old French hangart, *hamgart, from Old Frankish *haimgard (“fence around a group of houses”), from *haim (“home, village, hamlet”) + *gard (“yard”). ex.ja: 大型と小型の２台の飛行機が、ハンガー内で停止していました。

ex.ja: 彼は誰にも負けない勉強家だ。

en: Acting or done in haste; hurried or too quick; speedy due to having little time.
Made in haste.

hasty.ety: From Middle English hasty, of obscure origin. ex.ja: 私たちは急いで食事をすまし、すぐに出かけた。

ex.ja: 私は急いで朝食を食べて、家を出た。

ex.ja: 急いで結論を出す必要はない。

note.ja: haste（急ぎ）+ -y。「急いだ・軽率な」。

Burly, stout; sometimes as a modifier for boys' clothing sizes that fit a large waist or chest.

imitate.ety: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French imiter.

ex.en: Tom can imitate the singer to a hair.
ex.ja: トムはその歌手をそっくりまねできる。

ex.en: Children imitate their friends rather than their parents.
ex.ja: 子供は両親よりもむしろ友達の真似をする。

ex.ja: 自己自身であれ。他人のまねをするな。

note.ja: ラテン語 imitari（まねる）から。「まねる」。imitation と同じ。

Something that makes something else less than perfect; a blemish, impurity, error, etc.

imperfection.ety: From Old French imperfeccion, from Latin imperfectiōnem, accusative of imperfectiō, from in- + perfectiō. By surface analysis, im- + perfection.

ex.ja: 発言するたびにボロが出る。

note.ja: im（否定）+ per（完全に）+ fect（作る）+ ion。完全に作られていないこと →「欠点・不完全」。

en: Not likely to be true.
Not likely to happen.

improbable.ety: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, im- + probable.

ex.ja: 君の説明は見えすいている。とても本当とは思えないよ。

ex.ja: その話は本当とは思えない。

note.ja: im（否定）+ prob（証明する）+ able。証明できそうにない →「ありそうもない」。

The act of steeping or soaking a substance in liquid so as to extract medicinal or herbal qualities.

infusion.ety: From Middle English infusioun, from Old French infusion, from Latin infusio, infusionem (“a pouring into, a wetting, a dyeing, a flow”), from infundo.

note.ja: infuse（注ぎ込む）+ -sion。in + fundere（注ぐ）。fusion と同じ fus。

ex.ja: この時計は故障しているらしい。

ex.ja: ジャネット・ジャクソンは衣装の不具合で、見えてはいけないところが見えてしまった。

ex.ja: ワイヤレスマウスの調子が悪くなって、すぐに新しいものを注文した。

en: The action of mocking; ridicule, derision.
